title: 40%-off rack
topic: A friend checks per-item rounding on three 40%-off clearance items
blurb: Three messy price tags, 40% off each one, rounded per line — and they claim zero drift.
prompt: A friend texted this walking out of an outlet store. Tap a line if the math doesn't check out, or call it clean.

segments.label: The tags
segments.text: Grabbed three shirts off a 40%-off rack: tags were $24.98, $19.99, and $15.03 — $60.00 flat before the discount.

segments.label: The register
segments.text: The register takes 40% off each shirt separately and rounds every line to the nearest cent instead of discounting the $60 once.

segments.label: The total
segments.text: Funny thing is it still rang up to $36.00 on the nose — the tiny fraction-of-a-cent round-ups and round-downs canceled out.

segments.label: The change
segments.text: Handed over two twenties and got $4 back clean.

conclusion: Per-item rounding on $24.98, $19.99, and $15.03 at 40% off still sums to $36.00 flat.

diagnosis: $24.98 + $19.99 + $15.03 adds up to $59.90, not $60.00 flat, so the baseline is already off by a dime.
40% off $60.00 means you pay $24.00, not $36.00 — you used the discount instead of the sale price.
Outlet racks usually round tags to .99, so $15.03 already has sales tax baked into the tag.
Adding three tags before discounting hides that each shirt sits in a different clearance bracket.
fix: Re-add the three tags: $24.98 + $19.99 + $15.03 is $59.90, not $60.
Take 40% of $60 to get $24.00 as the checkout price.
Check each shirt's discount separately instead of summing to $60 first.
Add local sales tax before checking whether the total lands on an even dollar.

diagnosis: Taking 40% off three items separately compounds the discount instead of matching a single 40% cut.
Rounding three odd-cent items to the nearest penny always adds at least a penny of drift to the bill.

fix: Ask the cashier to apply 40% off once to the $60 subtotal to avoid compounding.

diagnosis: Two tags end in .98 and .99, so both round down and leave you at $35.99, a penny under $36.00.
40% off $60 is $24.00; paying $36.00 means the register only gave you a 24-dollar tag cut, wait — 60% off.
Per-item rounding errors are 0.2¢, 0.4¢, and 0.8¢, which can't cancel to an exact zero.
fix: Correct the checkout total from $36.00 to $24.00 for a 40%-off sale.
Note that you were overcharged by one cent from the two round-ups.

diagnosis: If the lines actually summed to $36.01, two twenties would give back $3.99, not $4 flat.
With sales tax on $36.00, two twenties wouldn't give you a clean $4 back.
Getting $4 back from $40 means you paid 60% off ($24) only if you handed over $28.
Paying with two twenties ($40) on a $35.99 bill should have returned $4.01.
fix: Check your pocket for the missing penny — $40 minus $35.99 is $4.01.
Check the receipt again: $36.01 leaves $3.99 in change, not $4.
Account for sales tax so the $4 change makes sense.
Verify the cashier didn't skip discounting the third shirt.
